_comment: The protocol, and the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for it (spec S4.4).
TypeScript interfaces and C++ parse/serialize code are BOTH generated from
this file by scripts/gen_protocol.py; the protocol ratchet regenerates and
diffs, so drift fails the build. A field that exists on one side only is a
build error, not a runtime mystery.
NAMESPACE. `lmp/*`, private, and honest about it. v1 called itself MCP,
implemented none of the handshake, and the only occurrence of `initialize`
in its transport was a parser warm-up string literal. This is not MCP and
does not claim to be (S4.4).

McpServerSettings._comment: Namespace for this server's tools, which register as mcp__<name>__<tool> -- so a remote `read_file` cannot shadow the native one.
McpServerSettings.name: name

McpServerSettings._comment: Extra environment for the server process, as KEY=VALUE entries.
McpServerSettings.name: env

McpServerSettings._comment: The operator vouching for this server. A remote tool runs in the SERVER's process, outside Seatbelt, so we cannot contain it -- untrusted servers therefore register every tool as irreversible and each call raises an approval card. trusted:true is a T3-class vouch: the extension requires a once-per-window modal acknowledgement, the sidecar logs the server executable/args hash, and every remote call invalidates workspace observation freshness. The server's own MCP annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint) are shown on that card as the server's claim and never decide anything: the MCP spec itself says they must not be trusted for security.
McpServerSettings.name: trusted

RunSettings._comment: Positive int32 only; negatives and overflows are refused at the sidecar boundary.
RunSettings.name: max_iterations

RunSettings._comment: Ceiling on a run's TOTAL duration. Positive int32 only; negatives and overflows are refused at the sidecar boundary. This is the runaway stop of last resort, not the dial that should normally end a run -- that is max_iterations. A run doing useful work for hours is not a fault, so this sits far above any honest run and stall_seconds catches the hangs.
RunSettings.name: wall_clock_seconds

RunSettings._comment: Seconds a run may go WITHOUT COMPLETING A TURN before it is stopped, reported as `stalled_no_turn`. Positive int32 only. Separate from wall_clock_seconds because 'this run is hung' and 'this run is long' are different questions and one number cannot answer both -- conflating them is what ended productive 48-turn runs at a 200-turn budget and made the operator retype `continue`.
RunSettings.name: stall_seconds

RunSettings._comment: 0 no execution, 1 macOS Seatbelt, 2 container (refuses until wired), 3 UNSANDBOXED on the host. The number is an identity, not a rank -- 3 is the least contained, not the most. Plan mode pins this to 0 whatever is asked for: a mode that cannot execute cannot be talked into executing by a settings field.
RunSettings.name: sandbox_tier

RunSettings._comment: false makes EVERY command execution raise a card, whatever its risk score. true keeps the risk-routed behaviour for ordinary commands (including toolchain drivers the classifier marks PartiallyParsed, such as `swift build`, so builds stay low-friction under T1). Irreversible capabilities, Unparseable status, and opaque script shapes (interpreter+file, source/eval) always escalate after this switch -- they are property overrides, not score bumps, so turning auto-approve on cannot wave `bash wipe.sh` through. Named for what the operator turns on -- 'run ordinary commands without asking me' -- rather than for the harness's internal routing.
RunSettings.name: auto_approve_exec

RunSettings._comment: false makes every workspace-mutating call raise a card. Writes had no HITL path at all before: mode policy decided whether they were allowed and nothing asked about any individual one.
RunSettings.name: auto_approve_writes

RunSettings._comment: The client can apply workspace edits itself, via lmp/edit + lmp/edit_applied (S12.4). The extension sets it so writes go through VS Code's WorkspaceEdit API and undo works; agent_eval.py and any other headless client leave it false and the sidecar writes directly. Advertised rather than assumed -- guessing wrong either wedges an unattended run on a reply nobody will send, or writes behind the editor's back.
RunSettings.name: applies_edits

RunSettings._comment: The client answers lmp/code_intel with language features VS Code already hosts (workspace symbols, definition, references, diagnostics, rename preview). locate_symbol routes through this when true; headless clients leave it false and keep the ranked filesystem walk. Not clangd-in-sidecar and not the post-edit syntax_check seam.
RunSettings.name: provides_code_intel

RunSettings._comment: Overrides the built-in persona. The editor keeps one per mode, so 'plan' can be told to think out loud and 'agent' to be terse. Empty means the built-in, which is the only reason this can be a plain string rather than a presence flag.
RunSettings.name: system_prompt

RunSettings._comment: Commands the operator has already said yes to, newline-separated (the generator has no array type, and a newline is the one character a shell command cannot contain unescaped). An entry matches a command that equals it, or that starts with it followed by a space. A command containing shell chaining -- ; && || | ` $( > < & -- NEVER matches, because `pytest` on the allowlist must not authorise `pytest; rm -rf ~`. Persistent prefix matches apply ONLY to fully parsed, non-destructive commands -- they cannot auto-approve irreversible capabilities or opaque script shapes (bash/python/source of a file, Unparseable). Toolchain drivers the classifier marks PartiallyParsed (`swift build`, `cmake --build`) are not on this list's path; auto_approve_exec covers their low-friction case under T1. Opaque run-scoped 'Always allow' binds to workspace + command + classifier caps + referenced script digests for the rest of THIS run only. Irreversible command cards do not offer Always allow.
RunSettings.name: allowed_commands

RunSettings._comment: Must be a positive int32. Negatives and overflows are refused at the sidecar boundary. When the loaded checkpoint publishes max_position_embeddings, this value is also clamped so prompt budget + reserved generation cannot exceed the model maximum.
RunSettings.name: context_budget_tokens

RunSettings._comment: The generation cap for ONE turn. AgentConfig has always had this field and the protocol never carried it, so it was pinned at 4096 for every run the editor or the driver could start -- the same wired-on-one-side-consumed-by-nobody shape as sandbox_tier and require_approval before them. MEASURED: a cold start on a five-task mission spent FIVE of its nine turns hitting the cap, produced no tool call on any of them, and ended length_capped_no_progress with an empty workspace. A capped turn leaves nothing behind (reasoning is not carried forward), so it is the one failure that can burn a whole budget while looking like the model is working. Raise it for missions that need a long first plan; it costs decode time per turn, not context. Must be a positive int32; refused when it alone exceeds the checkpoint maximum sequence length.
RunSettings.name: max_new_tokens

RunSettings._comment: How hard the model should think, as the CHECKPOINT defines it: `low`, `medium` or `xhigh`, or empty for the checkpoint's own default. Not a number and not a token cap -- Qwen3.8 implements these as one plain sentence at the top of the system prompt, and `medium` is the empty sentence, so the levels differ by the instruction given and not by any budget the harness enforces (max_new_tokens is the separate knob that does that). Only some checkpoints understand it: Qwen3.8-27B does, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has no reasoning_effort in its template at all, so the sidecar probes the checkpoint and drops the field rather than emitting an instruction the model was never trained on. Anything outside the three words is refused at the sidecar boundary -- the reference template raises on an unknown effort, and `high` in particular LOOKS valid and is not.
RunSettings.name: reasoning_effort

RunSettings._comment: THE OPERATOR'S CHECK -- the only verification the harness runs. When non-empty, the command runs verbatim after any turn that wrote a file, its output and exit status become an observation the model reads, and the run's final `completed` requires its last reading to have passed. Exit 0 is pass. Empty means no check: the run ends when the model answers. Operator-owned; the model cannot set or replace it.
RunSettings.name: verify_contract

RunSettings._comment: MCP servers to connect at run start. Each is spawned over stdio, initialized and asked for its tool list; a server that fails to start or answer leaves its tools ABSENT and the run continues, because a broken server must not be able to stall a turn.
RunSettings.name: mcp_servers

PerfSample._comment: Prompt tokens reused from the verified KV prefix rather than re-prefilled.
PerfSample.name: prefill_reused_tokens

SessionSummary._comment: The sidecar-minted run identity (see src/surface/run_id.hpp). Runs whose id is a legacy request counter are NOT listed: those ids collided across runs -- 97 runs over 6 values in the log this was built against -- so resuming one would splice unrelated conversations together.
SessionSummary.name: run_id

SessionSummary._comment: Wall-clock nanoseconds at run_begin. Sent as the raw stamp rather than a formatted date because 'when' is a rendering decision and the surface already turns it into '3h ago'.
SessionSummary.name: started_wall_ns

SessionSummary._comment: A run_end was seen. Its ABSENCE is the interesting case -- the process died mid-run, which is what resume exists for -- so this is reported rather than folded into `resumable`.
SessionSummary.name: finished

SessionSummary._comment: How many observations a resume would restore. Zero means there is nothing to return to however healthy the run looks, which is why the surface shows it.
SessionSummary.name: observations

TranscriptEntry._comment: "user", "assistant" or "tool" -- the three shapes the pane already paints for a live run. Kept as a role string rather than split into three arrays so the ORDER of the conversation survives the wire, which is the whole point of sending it.
TranscriptEntry.name: role

TranscriptEntry._comment: Tool name and its one-line argument preview, both empty unless role is "tool". These are what the live turn row shows in its summary, so a resumed row can be built from the same parts.
TranscriptEntry.name: tool

TranscriptEntry._comment: This entry's text was cut to fit. Said per entry rather than once for the whole transcript because the reader needs to know WHICH observation they are seeing part of -- a silently shortened file is indistinguishable from a short file.
TranscriptEntry.name: truncated

params._comment: Images to show the model with this message, as workspace-relative paths. PATHS, not bytes: the surface writes a dropped or pasted image into the workspace and sends where it put it, so the picture travels the same route as a file the model opened itself -- decoded and patched at prompt time, re-readable by view_image in a later turn, and never a megabyte of base64 on a wire format that would then have to carry it in every replayed transcript. A path outside the workspace is refused at the sidecar boundary, like every other path.
params.name: image_paths

lmp/cancel._comment: MUST be deliverable while the model is generating (S4.3). The reader thread parses the method field of a COMPLETE message and sets the cancel token; no substring matching on transport bytes, ever.

lmp/edit_applied._comment: The editor's answer to lmp/edit. Applied through VS Code's WorkspaceEdit API so undo, dirty buffers and diff review all work (S12.4); `applied:false` carries the reason and becomes a tool error, so a refusal in the editor is a fact the model can act on rather than a silent no-op.

lmp/code_intel_result._comment: The editor's answer to lmp/code_intel. result_text is path:line: detail lines (same shape as locate_symbol) or a diagnostics listing; the sidecar BLOCKS on it the same way it blocks on edit_applied.

params._comment: The operator consenting to the REST OF THIS RUN's whole-file writes, from the card in front of them. Scoped to the run and never persisted. Why a run scope rather than a per-path allowlist like `allowed_commands`: the two gates have opposite repeat behaviour. A command recurs verbatim -- `pytest` is the same string every turn -- so remembering it saves every later click. A path does not: a run rewriting eleven scaffolded stubs writes eleven DIFFERENT paths once each, so a per-path rule can only ever be created after its one and only use, and the operator still answers eleven cards. MEASURED: exactly that, eleven write_file cards in one ResMon run with auto_approve_writes on. Applied in the sidecar's approver rather than as a config field because it has to take effect on the NEXT CARD of the SAME run -- an allowlist entry written to editor settings only reaches the sidecar at the next lmp/start, which is one run too late to help the run that asked.
params.name: allow_writes_for_run

params._comment: The 'Always allow' button's OTHER half, for the run that is asking. The rule itself is persisted by the extension into `allowedCommands` for ordinary fully-parsed commands -- but settings reach the sidecar at the next lmp/start, so within the run that raised the card the identical command escalates again and the button reads as broken. MEASURED: an operator clicked 'Always allow' on a build command and answered the same card on the next turn. Latched here for the rest of the run and never persisted (the persistent copy is the extension's); the two halves are deliberately separate, because one has to survive the run and the other has to take effect inside it. Fully-parsed commands match VERBATIM. Opaque (PartiallyParsed / Unparseable) commands latch a key of workspace + command + classifier capabilities + digests of referenced script files, so approving `bash build.sh` does not survive a rewrite of build.sh. Irreversible command cards do not offer Always allow at all.
params.name: allow_command_for_run

_comment: Talk to the agent. ONE method, two behaviours, decided by whether a run is
in flight -- because from the user's side there is only one act, 'say
something to it', and which of those two it turns out to be is the
harness's business rather than the caller's.
IN FLIGHT: steering. The text lands in the run's context at the NEXT TURN
BOUNDARY, not mid-generation. Cancel is the violent one and sets a token
mid-token-stream; steering is gentle by design, so the model finishes the
thought it is having and reads the instruction before choosing its next
move. It also marks the plan stale, which makes `plan` the only callable
tool on the following turn -- so an instruction cannot be received and
then quietly ignored (S9.2: mechanism, not a sentence asking it to listen).
IDLE: a follow-up. The same ContextStore, the same loaded weights, one more
user turn. `started_run` says which happened, and `run_id` names the run
the text went to either way.

params._comment: Images to show the model with this message, as workspace-relative paths. PATHS, not bytes: the surface writes a dropped or pasted image into the workspace and sends where it put it, so the picture travels the same route as a file the model opened itself -- decoded and patched at prompt time, re-readable by view_image in a later turn, and never a megabyte of base64 on a wire format that would then have to carry it in every replayed transcript. A path outside the workspace is refused at the sidecar boundary, like every other path.
params.name: image_paths

_comment: Load the weights, as its own act.
The load used to be a side effect of lmp/start: the first mission of a
session paid ~19 GB of it, after the reply had already been sent, with no
notification of any kind. From the editor that was a minute of a status
line reading 'Thinking' about a model that did not exist yet, and a
checkpoint that could not be opened produced its only symptom at the end
of a run that never began.
Separating it gives the operator the thing they actually want to control --
WHEN 19 GB of unified memory is taken, on a machine that has 48 -- and gives
the surface a state to render. lmp/start still loads on demand if nothing is
loaded, so no client is required to call this first; it is the explicit door
into the same room, not a new precondition.
Progress is reported by lmp/model_status notifications, not by this reply:
the reply cannot arrive until the load has finished, and 'it is working' is
only useful before then.

result._comment: Empty on success. Carries the tokenizer's or the backend's own refusal text otherwise -- 'MLX is not compiled into this build', a missing safetensors -- because a load failure is nearly always a fixable statement about the checkpoint on disk and paraphrasing it would throw that away.
result.name: error

_comment: Give the memory back, without killing the process.
The pair to lmp/load_model, and not a nicety: one checkpoint is ~19 GB on a
48 GB host, so 'I need that memory for something else' is a routine request
and the only answer used to be closing the editor. The conversation dies with
the weights -- a context store whose model has gone is not resumable -- so
this is a real reset, and the surface says so before it sends one.

lmp/sessions._comment: The runs this workspace can return to, newest first, derived from the event log rather than from a side index -- the log is what resume replays, so a session listed here can always be rebuilt. `workspace_root` filters to the caller's workspace: run history is per-repo, and offering another project's conversations would be both noise and a leak.

params._comment: 0 or absent means the sidecar's own default cap. A listing is a UI affordance, not a query API.
params.name: limit

lmp/resume._comment: Reload a previous run's conversation into this session WITHOUT re-executing any tool. The context is rebuilt from the event log; the run does not restart, so the operator sees the history and then continues it with lmp/message. Refused when the bound identity no longer matches (different workspace, model, protocol or tool schema) or when an edit was in flight when the run died -- resuming across either would put the model in a conversation about a world that no longer exists.

params._comment: The same settings lmp/start takes: the model may not be loaded, and the resumed session has to run under a known configuration rather than whatever the last run left behind.
params.name: settings

result._comment: Empty on success; otherwise the refusal in the resume gate's own words, which name which bound field changed.
result.name: why

result._comment: Observations restored into the context. The surface shows this because 'resumed' with a zero here is a real outcome and looks identical to success otherwise.
result.name: turns_restored

result._comment: The restored conversation, oldest first, for the pane to repaint. BOUNDED: a single observation in the real log reaches 708 KB, so entries are capped individually and the whole transcript is capped again, oldest entries dropped first. The model's context is unaffected -- this is only what the surface is shown.
result.name: transcript

result._comment: How many leading entries were dropped to fit the cap. Non-zero means the pane is showing the TAIL of a longer conversation, which it must say rather than imply the run began where the paint begins.
result.name: omitted_leading

lmp/model_status._comment: The ONLY thing that says whether this process can answer a prompt. It is sent on every transition, and once unsolicited right after lmp/ready, so a surface that attaches at any moment learns the truth without asking -- rather than inferring 'loaded' from the absence of an error, which is how a run came to sit on 'Thinking' for a minute with no model behind it.
lmp/model_status.name: state

lmp/model_status._comment: Empty except on `failed`, where it is the loader's verbatim refusal.
lmp/model_status.name: detail

lmp/model_status._comment: How long the load took, on `ready` and `failed`. Measured, so the surface can tell the operator what a reload of THIS checkpoint on THIS machine actually costs instead of guessing at a spinner.
lmp/model_status.name: elapsed_ms

lmp/model_status._comment: Whether THIS checkpoint's chat template understands reasoning_effort. Sent because the surface cannot work it out -- both checkpoints here are Family::Qwen3 and only one has the levels -- and because the alternative is a control that looks live and does nothing. The sidecar already drops an unsupported effort silently and logs why; that is the right behaviour for a settings file shared across checkpoints, and exactly the wrong thing to render as an enabled button. Rides model_status rather than a reply because it is a property of the loaded checkpoint and has to survive a surface attaching late, which is the same argument `state` makes.
lmp/model_status.name: supports_reasoning_effort

lmp/turn._comment: Tokens routed by the grammar into private reasoning prose.
lmp/turn.name: think_tokens

lmp/turn._comment: Tokens routed by the grammar into answer prose.
lmp/turn.name: text_tokens

lmp/turn._comment: Generated tokens routed into neither prose channel: tool XML and structural delimiters.
lmp/turn.name: tool_tokens

lmp/turn._comment: Zero-based position of this tool row in one model-emitted batch.
lmp/turn.name: batch_index

lmp/turn._comment: Number of tool calls emitted in this turn; zero for text-only turns.
lmp/turn.name: batch_count

lmp/turn._comment: Workspace-content bytes consumed by this read tool, when measured.
lmp/turn.name: read_bytes

lmp/turn._comment: Bytes added plus removed by this edit tool, when measured.
lmp/turn.name: edit_bytes

lmp/turn._comment: Grammar phase where a length-capped generation stopped; empty otherwise.
lmp/turn.name: cap_phase

lmp/verification._comment: Whether the command EXECUTED at all. false means the reading says nothing about the workspace -- the command was refused by the sandbox or does not exist here (exit 126/127) -- and the UI must render that as a fact about the check, not as a failure of the work.
lmp/verification.name: ran

lmp/verification._comment: The command's exit status, verbatim. A report, never a verdict: the harness runs the operator's check and says what it did.
lmp/verification.name: passed

lmp/approval_request._comment: The command verbatim, when there is one. `preview` truncates each argument at 120 characters for display, so it is the wrong thing to remember an allowlist rule from -- a truncated rule would either never match again or, worse, match something shorter than what was approved.
lmp/approval_request.name: command

lmp/approval_request._comment: Whether this call carries a capability that cannot be undone. Computed by the loop and sent, rather than re-derived in the view from the chips, so the UI and the gate cannot disagree about which calls are unwaivable.
lmp/approval_request.name: irreversible

lmp/approval_request._comment: Whether 'Always allow' could persist a rule that will ever match again -- see loop::can_persist_allowlist_rule. Computed by the gate and sent for the same reason `irreversible` is: the view must not re-derive it. A command carrying shell chaining (`;` `|` `&&`) or one the classifier could not fully parse can never be matched by a stored prefix, and the button used to be offered anyway: MEASURED, 19 rules written to one workspace's settings, none of them reachable, against a run that answered 35 cards. When this is false the card offers run-scoped consent instead, which the sidecar honours on the very next turn.
lmp/approval_request.name: can_remember

lmp/edit._comment: Matched by the lmp/edit_applied reply, the same shape a card uses. The sidecar BLOCKS on it: the tool result has to say whether the bytes landed, and an unanswered edit that reported success would leave the model editing a file nothing wrote.
lmp/edit.name: request_id

lmp/edit._comment: Optimistic-concurrency preimage: SHA-256 hex of the bytes the edit was computed against. Empty when expected_absent is true (create). The extension compares this to the in-memory TextDocument, not disk alone.
lmp/edit.name: expected_version

lmp/edit._comment: Create claim: the path must not exist in the editor (or on disk when first opened). Mutually exclusive with a non-empty expected_version.
lmp/edit.name: expected_absent

lmp/code_intel._comment: Matched by lmp/code_intel_result. op is one of workspace_symbols, definition, references, diagnostics, rename_preview. Uses the language services the editor already hosts — not a sidecar clangd.
lmp/code_intel.name: request_id

lmp/run_end._comment: Checklist items still open when the run ended. The checklist is the model's own progress display and holds no authority over the ending; this field reports what it said, so completed=true with unfinished_items>0 is visible to the human rather than resolved silently.
lmp/run_end.name: unfinished_items

lmp/notice._comment: A degradation the run SURVIVED, told to the operator instead of only to the event log. There is a class of these and they all failed the same way: the context journal not opening, an MCP server not connecting. Each is deliberately non-fatal -- wedging an agent because a disk is full or a server is down would be a worse trade -- and each was therefore invisible, because the only record was a line in a log nobody reads unless they already suspect something. A run that quietly lost its durable context behaves subtly worse for the rest of its life and never says so. This is the channel that says so.
lmp/notice.name: run_id

lmp/notice._comment: Stable machine-readable identifier, so a surface can decide how to render one without matching on prose.
lmp/notice.name: code

lmp/notice._comment: `warning` means the run continues with something switched off. `error` is reserved for a notice that also ends the run, so a surface can style the two differently without inspecting the code.
lmp/notice.name: severity

lmp/notice._comment: What the notice is ABOUT -- a path, a server name. Separate from `detail` so a surface can show the short thing and keep the long one for a tooltip.
lmp/notice.name: subject

lmp/notice._comment: Verbatim underlying reason, never a paraphrase. "unable to open database file" tells an operator which of two causes they have; "context unavailable" does not.
lmp/notice.name: detail
